content: Paragonimus is a parasitic lung fluke, a type of flatworm. Infection occurs when a person consumes raw or undercooked freshwater crabs or crayfish that are infected with the parasite. If the fluke migrates to the central nervous system, it can cause severe symptoms that resemble meningitis. Paragonimus infection is caused by over 30 species of trematodes belonging to the genus Paragonimus. Among these, Paragonimus westermani, also known as the oriental lung fluke, is the most common species infecting humans. The distribution of Paragonimus species spans the Americas, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Paragonimus westermani is primarily found in Southeast Asia and Japan, while Paragonimus kellicotti is endemic to North America. The clinical presentation of chronic paragonimiasis can mimic chronic bronchitis or tuberculosis. Patients may experience coughing with coffee-colored or blood-tinged sputum, often accompanied by chest pain and/or shortness of breath. Paragonimiasis typically begins as an acute infection, presenting with symptoms such as cough, abdominal pain, discomfort, and low-grade fever, which may appear 2 to 15 days after infection. In most cases, the infection resolves without treatment. Individuals with mild infections may remain asymptomatic. However, long-term infections can resemble bronchitis or tuberculosis, with symptoms such as coughing up blood-tinged sputum. Central nervous system involvement occurs in up to 25% of hospitalized patients and may manifest as Paragonimus-induced meningitis. Diagnosis is confirmed by microscopic identification of eggs in stool or sputum, although these eggs are not detectable until 2 to 3 months after infection. Eggs may also occasionally be found in effusion fluid or biopsy samples. Concentration techniques may be required for patients with light infections. Biopsy can provide diagnostic confirmation and species identification if an adult or developing fluke is recovered. Chest X-rays often reveal a range of abnormalities, including lobar infiltrates, coin lesions, cavities, calcified nodules, hilar enlargement, pleural thickening, and effusions. A characteristic finding is the presence of ring-shaped opacities from contiguous cavities, resembling a bunch of grapes, which is highly suggestive of pulmonary paragonimiasis. Computed tomography (CT) imaging of the brain may reveal similar grape bunch findings in cases of central nervous system involvement, particularly in the temporal and occipital lobes. The treatment of choice for paragonimiasis is praziquantel. Bithionol is an alternative medication for treating this condition. To prevent infection, individuals should avoid consuming raw freshwater crabs or crayfish. These crustaceans should be cooked to an internal temperature of at least 145°F (~63°C). Travelers should be advised to avoid traditional dishes that include undercooked freshwater crustaceans.
